newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian democracy seen coming of age.
newsitem.headline: Indian democracy seen coming of age.

text.p: India withstood three weeks of political convulsions with aplomb, reflecting the maturity of the world's most populous democracy in its 50th year, politicians and analysts said on Wednesday.
Prime Minister Inder Kumar Gujral won a vote of confidence in parliament on Tuesday, putting an end to a 24-day political crisis that yielded India's fourth prime minister in a year.
But the nation, numbering some 936 million citizens speaking more than a dozen official languages, took the change of governments in stride, analysts and politicians said.
"It is a sign of self-confidence of people and maturity," V.A. Pai Panandikar, director of the Centre for Policy Research (CPR), told Reuters.
"It was an eloquent indication of maturity of democratic polity in India," said United Front spokesman Jaipal Reddy.
Gujral was elected leader of the United Front coalition on Saturday after his party colleague and former prime minister H.D. Deve Gowda lost a confidence vote on April 11.

The political crisis was triggered when the Congress party decided to withdraw support for Deve Gowda's government on March 30. Congress later pledged support to the new United Front alliance under Gujral's leadership.

"It did not have to be proved. But India showed once again that democracy has taken root in a multi-ethnic society and a linguistically divided country," columnist Kuldip Nayar wrote in The Hindustan Times newspaper.
"The political crisis in the country caused no tension, no confrontation, no untoward incident."

Analysts attributed the maturity to deep democratic roots and the stable functioning of state institutions, some of which date back to British rule. True parliamentary democracy began with independence from Britain in 1947.
"People have come to realise whatever problems are there at the government level, the state's structure is sound and stable," said Panandikar.

The judiciary had risen to the challenge in recent years, probing corruption charges against leaders of various political parties, he said. That had boosted confidence in the nation's institutional framework.
"The system has struck deep roots and is capable of withstanding seismic shocks," Reddy said.
"We can change government...but the system goes on, democracy continues and strengthens," Gujral said in his maiden speech after being sworn in as prime minister on Monday.

The political turmoil did jolt financial markets. The markets were especially worried over the fate of the 1997/98 (April-March) budget presented by former finance minister P. Chidambaram in February.
The budget has been widely hailed by industry and foreign investors for slashing corporate and personal income taxes, and lowering import tariffs.
A consensus among political parties to approve the budget in parliament, perhaps with some amendments, was yet another indication of maturity, analysts said.
"We may not be rated very high economically," Panandikar said. "But we certainly rate very high on a political development scale."
